topic: Peter Wason (1966/1968): The Four-Card Puzzle ('E — K — 4 — 7') That Stumps 90% of Educated Adults
visual_mode_reason: Peter Wason's 1966/1968 four-card tabletop puzzle ('E, K, 4, 7' testing 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other') is pure cognitive logic and confirmation bias made visually gripping on a physical felt tabletop.

primary_case.title: Peter Cathcart Wason's 1966/1968 University College London 4-Card Selection Task ('E — K — 4 — 7')
primary_case.place: Psycholinguistics Research Unit, University College London

people.name: Peter Cathcart Wason
people.role: UCL cognitive psychologist (and chess player) who coined 'confirmation bias' and designed both the 2-4-6 rule test and the 4-card selection task

people.name: Philip N. Johnson-Laird
people.role: Wason's UCL collaborator who co-tested stubborn rationalizations when people are shown the hidden backs of the cards

people.name: Jonathan St. B. T. Evans & Leda Cosmides
people.role: Researchers whose 'matching bias' eye-tracking studies and 'drinking-age social contract' flips revealed WHY abstract cards fool 90% of people

core_facts.fact: In 1966-1968 at University College London, Peter Wason laid FOUR double-sided cards flat on a table — showing **E**, **K**, **4**, and **7** (or D, K, 3, 7) — with one guarantee: every card has a letter on one side and a number on the other.
Participants had to test ONE simple rule by turning over ONLY the minimum necessary cards: **'If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side.'**
Across university students, professors, and even trained mathematicians caught off guard, **fewer than 10%** (typically 4% to 10%) picked the logically correct pair (**E and 7**).
Instead, roughly **45-50%** picked **E and 4**, and another ~35% picked **E alone**.

Why is **4** a complete waste of a flip while **7** is mandatory? Flipping **4** and finding a consonant like 'K' does NOT break the rule (the rule never forbade consonants from having even numbers!); ONLY finding a vowel hiding behind the odd number **7** ('E on one side, 7 on the other!') can FALSIFY the rule (*modus tollens*: if P to Q, check P and NOT-Q).

In Wason's 1968/1969 follow-ups, even when experimenters let students turn over **7**, stare right at a vowel on the back, and asked if **7** mattered, many stubbornly insisted 'No, only E and 4 matter!' until walked step-by-step through the contradiction.

Yet change the EXACT same logical rule from abstract 'E-K-4-7' to a concrete rule-violation check — Johnson-Laird's 1972 British postal rule ('If a letter is sealed, it must carry a 50-lire stamp') or Griggs & Cox's 1982 pub rule (**'If a person is drinking beer, they must be over 21'**: cards `Drinking Beer`, `Drinking Soda`, `Age 25`, `Age 16`) — and **75% to 85% of people instantly nail `Drinking Beer` and `Age 16`**.

Jonathan Evans (1984) discovered a second sneaky culprit alongside confirmation bias: **'Matching Bias'** — our eyes reflexively grab the two words explicitly mentioned in the sentence ('vowel' — E, 'even number' — 4), which is why negating the rule ('If vowel, then NOT even') ironically makes people pick the right card by accident.

While roughly 90% of adults fail Wason's abstract E-K-4-7 card rule (<10% choosing E and 7, echoing Wason's 1960 '2-4-6' rule-discovery task), Griggs and Cox's (1982) drinking-age rule raised logical falsification accuracy toward ~75–80%.

wow_facts.fact: Four index cards on a desk — **E, K, 4, 7** — and 90% of university students, doctors, and PhDs reach straight for **E and 4** while completely ignoring **7**, the ONLY second card capable of proving the rule wrong.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Four cardboard squares exposed a universal blind spot in human reasoning.

wow_facts.fact: Swap 'Vowel to Even' for a pub bouncer's rule — **'If drinking beer, must be over 21'** (`Beer`, `Soda`, `25`, `16`) — and suddenly nobody flips `Age 25`. Everyone instantly checks `Beer` and `Age 16` (the exact twin of `E` and `7`).
wow_facts.why_surprising: Human logic isn't broken — it is wired for catching rule-breakers, not abstract symbols.

wow_facts.fact: In Wason's earlier '2-4-6' cousin test, people guessed '8-10-12!', '20-22-24!', '100-102-104!' hearing 'Yes' every time and swore the secret rule was 'even numbers +2' — never once testing '1-2-3' to learn the real rule was simply 'any ascending numbers'.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Confirmation bias: piling up 'Yeses' feels smart while teaching you zero.

wow_facts.fact: Even after physically flipping **7** and seeing a rule-breaking **E** printed on the back, half of Wason's 1969 volunteers initially tried to talk their way out of admitting **7** mattered.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Once our brain locks onto a pet answer, we lawyer for it.

misconceptions.myth: Failing E-K-4-7 means someone has low intelligence or poor education.
misconceptions.truth: High-IQ graduate students and professors miss E-K-4-7 at roughly 85-90% on first sight because fast intuitive attention ('matching + positive test strategy') grabs 'E' and '4' before slow formal deduction wakes up.

misconceptions.myth: Good scientists and analysts prove their hypothesis by gathering as many confirming examples as possible.
misconceptions.truth: Confirming cases ('4 has an E!') are often cheap; Karl Popper and Peter Wason showed real confidence comes ONLY from surviving deliberate attempts to FALSIFY ('flipping the 7').

misconceptions.myth: Abstract logic courses automatically cure everyday confirmation bias.
misconceptions.truth: Even trained logicians slip unless they translate abstract claims into concrete 'what evidence would prove me WRONG?' checks.

everyday_hooks: Googling 'why intermittent fasting / my favorite stock works' (flipping the 4) instead of 'strongest evidence against my stock thesis' (flipping the 7).
Diagnosing a software bug or patient symptom by checking only tests that match your first hunch.
Instantly spotting who to card as a bartender (`Beer` + `16-year-old`) after getting tricked two minutes earlier by `E — K — 4 — 7`.
